plan.angle: Keep the same structure and title. Chapter 4: cite only persistence studies you can locate and open (for example Gasoyan 2026 DOM doi 10.1111/dom.70660; Ulrich 2026 DOM doi 10.1111/dom.70535, which is GLP-1 receptor agonists in type 2 diabetes with no tirzepatide). Label each one 'observational' and name the drugs and population it covered. Drop the 'DOCC' citation unless the Scriptwriter can find and verify the actual paper. Say that cost and access drove many discontinuations. Present SURMOUNT-4 regain as group averages from weeks 36 to 88, and source the 'biology, not willpower' line to mechanism or label sources, not to SURMOUNT-4. Keep the guideline habits (strength training, protein with the kidney caveat) framed as 'recommended', not 'proven to prevent regain'.
plan.working_title: What Happens When You Stop Tirzepatide?
plan.why: A named playbook Lane A example (Lane A median 26, Strength Training growing) with high search demand. The randomized SURMOUNT-4 evidence holds up under fact-check, and the new real-world persistence papers give it a timely hook. | fact-check: The core topic is fine for Lane A. SURMOUNT-4 (Aronne et al., JAMA 2024) is a real randomized withdrawal trial in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes: a 36-week open-label lead-in, then randomization to continued tirzepatide or placebo for weeks 36 to 88. Take every per-arm % change, n and estimand from the JAMA paper. Chapter 3 is fine if it only uses the secondary outcomes the paper reports. The problem is chapter 4. I could not find an 'Oct 2026 Diabetes Obes Metab' persistence paper or any study called 'DOCC'. The real-world discontinuation papers I could confirm are: (a) Gasoyan et al. 2026, Diabetes Obes Metab, doi 10.1111/dom.70660, the Cleveland Clinic study of weight change after stopping semaglutide or tirzepatide (observational; most people went on to other obesity treatments); (b) Ulrich et al. 2026, Diabetes Obes Metab, doi 10.1111/dom.70535, a UK cohort of GLP-1 receptor agonists in type 2 diabetes. It covers dulaglutide and semaglutide, with no tirzepatide, and found a 41.1% one-year discontinuation risk; (c) the PMC12515774 academic obesity clinic paper, where only 5% of patients were on tirzepatide. Cost and access were major reasons people stopped in the real-world data, so don't frame stopping as a personal failing. Keep 'regain' as an average result, not something that happens to everyone. Keep the appetite biology to mechanism sources, not to SURMOUNT-4, which measured weight and not hunger. The ending CTA must name 'Strength Training on Tirzepatide' by its exact live title, oEmbed-verified.

package.description:
Quick answer: In SURMOUNT-4 (JAMA, online December 2023; adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, no diabetes), people switched from tirzepatide to placebo at week 36 regained 14.0% of body weight on average by week 88, but still ended 9.9% below their starting weight on average. Those who stayed on tirzepatide lost a further 5.5% (main analysis). Most common side effects on tirzepatide: nausea, diarrhea, constipation and vomiting.

Not personal advice. Please don't stop or change your medicine on your own, and talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
SURMOUNT-4 (JAMA): https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2023.24945
US stopping study (JAMA Netw Open): https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57349
UK persistence study (Diabetes Obes Metab): https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.70535
Cleveland Clinic study: https://newsroom.clevelandclinic.org/2026/03/12/what-happens-when-patients-stop-taking-glp-1-drugs-new-cleveland-clinic-study-reveals-real-world-insights

script.working_title: What Happens When You Stop Tirzepatide?
script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' scenario plus an open loop: the returning 10 p.m. food noise, then a promised 'hopeful number most headlines skip' that pays off in 'Is any weight loss kept?'

scenes.narration: Picture this. A few weeks after your last tirzepatide shot, it's ten at night, the kitchen is quiet, and the food thoughts you'd almost forgotten are suddenly loud again.

If you've wondered what happens when you stop tirzepatide, the best evidence gives a clear first answer. In a randomized trial, people switched to placebo regained weight on average, while people who stayed on it kept losing.
scenes.retention_device: First concrete answer in the first 15 seconds

scenes.narration: In the next few minutes, you'll learn how much weight came back, why appetite returns, how often people stop in real life, and what experts recommend to protect your progress.
scenes.on_screen_text: What you'll know by the end

scenes.narration: And there's one number in this trial that most headlines skip. It's the most hopeful result in the whole paper, and I'll show it to you near the end.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop (paid off in 'Is any weight loss kept?')

scenes.narration: One quick thing first. This is not personal advice. Please don't stop or change your medicine on your own; talk to your doctor or prescriber about what's right for you.
The trial is called SURMOUNT four. It was published in the journal JAMA, online in December two thousand twenty-three, and it asked one blunt question: what happens if you stop?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card framed as a searched question

scenes.narration: It enrolled adults with obesity, or with overweight plus a weight-related health condition, and none had diabetes. On average they were forty-eight years old, and about seven in ten were women.
Stage one lasted thirty-six weeks. Everyone took tirzepatide openly, building up to the highest dose they could tolerate, either ten or fifteen milligrams once a week.
scenes.retention_device: Step-by-step micro-story of the trial design

scenes.narration: Seven hundred eighty-three people began. The six hundred seventy who completed that stage had lost twenty point nine percent of their body weight, on average.
Then came the clever part. Those six hundred seventy people were randomly split into two groups of three hundred thirty-five.

visual.stock_query: crowd splitting into two equal groups

scenes.narration: One group kept getting tirzepatide. The other was switched to a placebo injection, and neither the participants nor the researchers knew who was in which group.
Both groups kept the same diet and activity counseling. So for the next fifty-two weeks, the big difference was the medicine itself.
At week eighty-eight, the two groups looked very different. Before I show you, take a guess. How much of the lost weight do you think came back?
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer and mini-cliffhanger before chapter change

scenes.narration: Here's the answer, and it's the main result of the whole trial.
In the group switched to placebo, body weight went up by fourteen percent on average between week thirty-six and week eighty-eight.

visual.stat_label: Placebo group, weeks 36–88, average weight change

scenes.narration: In the group that stayed on tirzepatide, weight kept falling, by another five point five percent on average over the same year.

visual.stat_label: Tirzepatide group, weeks 36–88, average weight change

scenes.narration: That's a gap of nineteen point four percentage points. These figures come from the trial's main analysis, which counts everyone randomized, whether or not they kept taking their assigned treatment.
To make that feel real, imagine Dana, forty-seven. She's hypothetical, and she starts at two hundred twenty pounds. A twenty point nine percent drop takes her to about one hundred seventy-four.
If she then matched the placebo group's average regain of fourteen percent, about twenty-four pounds would come back.
But averages hide a wide range. Some people on placebo regained more than that, and some regained much less.
At week eighty-eight, eighty-nine point five percent of people on tirzepatide had kept at least eighty percent of the weight they'd lost, versus sixteen point six percent on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Kept ≥80% of loss: tirzepatide vs placebo
visual.stock_query: two pie charts side by side

scenes.narration: So roughly one in six people on placebo still held on to most of their loss. The trial wasn't designed to explain what set them apart, but regain wasn't everyone's story.

And it's not just tirzepatide. In the STEP one trial extension, adults with overweight or obesity and no diabetes who stopped semaglutide regained about two-thirds of their earlier weight loss within a year.

visual.stat_label: Semaglutide stopped: share of loss regained, 1 year

scenes.retention_device: Corroborating evidence from a second trial

scenes.narration: Separate drug, separate trial, not head-to-head. Same direction.
So weight tends to come back after stopping. The real question is why. And if you've ever blamed yourself for that, stay with me, because the biology tells a different story.
scenes.retention_device: Emotional open loop and cliffhanger before chapter

scenes.narration: Let's start with the hormone these medicines are built around.
After you eat, your gut releases its own G L P one. It helps signal fullness to your brain, slows how fast your stomach empties, and helps your pancreas release insulin when blood sugar rises.
But your natural G L P one is short-lived. An enzyme called D P P four breaks it down within a couple of minutes.
Tirzepatide is engineered to last far longer. It activates two hormone receptors, G I P and G L P one, and its half-life is about five days. That's why it's a once-weekly shot.
Its prescribing information says tirzepatide lowers body weight by reducing calorie intake, likely by affecting appetite.
So when the weekly doses stop, the medicine gradually clears from the body over the following weeks, and the appetite effect it was providing fades with it.
But here's where it gets weird. The appetite you return to may be stronger than the one you started with.
In a classic New England Journal of Medicine study, researchers in Australia followed people with overweight or obesity who lost weight on a ten-week very low-calorie diet. No medicine involved.
A year later, the hunger hormone ghrelin was still higher than before, fullness hormones like leptin and peptide Y Y were still lower, and people reported feeling hungrier.
That was a diet study, not a tirzepatide study, so its numbers don't transfer. But it shows the body tends to defend lost weight with more hunger and less fullness.

visual.stock_query: body gently pushing back a door

scenes.narration: So if anyone's told you regain is simply a lack of willpower, the science says otherwise. Appetite is biology, and after weight loss, that biology pushes back.

visual.myth: MYTH: Regain after stopping is a willpower failure
visual.fact: After weight loss, appetite hormones push back

scenes.narration: Back to Dana. If her food noise returns after stopping, that's not a character flaw. It's what this research would predict, and it deserves a plan, not shame.
And weight wasn't the only thing that moved in SURMOUNT four. Some of the numbers your doctor checks shifted too.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop before chapter change

scenes.narration: During the first thirty-six weeks on tirzepatide, measures like waist size and blood pressure improved on average.

visual.stock_query: tape measure and blood pressure cuff

scenes.narration: After the switch, many of those measures drifted back toward where they started in the placebo group, while they held up better in people who stayed on tirzepatide.
These were secondary results, so treat them as supporting evidence, not the trial's headline finding.
What about side effects on tirzepatide in this trial? The most common were stomach-related, like nausea, diarrhea, constipation and vomiting.
scenes.retention_device: Question the viewer is already asking

scenes.narration: They were mostly mild to moderate, and mostly happened while doses were being increased in the first stage. If they bother you, your prescriber can help.
But here's the bigger surprise. Outside of trials, in everyday life, stopping turns out to be remarkably common.
Clinical trials are tidy. Real life isn't. So researchers dig through health records to see what people actually do.
Quick caution: these are observational studies. They show real-world patterns, but they can't prove cause and effect.
One large US study in JAMA Network Open followed adults with overweight or obesity who started semaglutide or liraglutide, two G L P one medicines.

visual.stock_query: map of USA with data dots

scenes.narration: Among those without type two diabetes, sixty-four point eight percent stopped within a year. Among people with type two diabetes, it was forty-six point five percent.

visual.stat_label: Stopped within 1 year, no type 2 diabetes

scenes.narration: A UK study of adults with type two diabetes starting a G L P one medicine, mostly dulaglutide or semaglutide, with no tirzepatide in the data, estimated a forty-one point one percent risk of stopping within a year.

visual.stat_label: UK, type 2 diabetes, GLP-1 starters (mostly dulaglutide or semaglutide): 1-year stopping risk

scenes.retention_device: Second data point, scope clearly labelled

scenes.narration: And a Cleveland Clinic study looked at real-world health records of adults who stopped semaglutide or tirzepatide. In the year after stopping, about one in four switched to a different medicine, one in five restarted the same one, and others used lifestyle programs.
scenes.retention_device: Unexpected twist that partly answers the regain worry

scenes.narration: Among people treated for obesity, who had lost about eight percent before stopping, average regain a year later was small, about half a percent, though more than half did gain some weight. The researchers think restarting and switching help explain why.

items: Obesity group: lost ~8.4%, then about +0.5% at 1 year
More than half gained some weight
Restarting and switching may explain it

scenes.retention_device: Honest context on the real-world regain number

scenes.narration: Observational, so it can't prove cause and effect. But it suggests stopping one medicine is often a step in a longer journey, not the end of the road.
Why do so many people stop? Records can't fully say, but two patterns stand out: side effects, and signs that cost and access matter.
In the JAMA Network Open study, people with higher incomes were less likely to stop. Health records can't tell us every reason, but that pattern points to affordability.
So if you stopped because of a price, a coverage change or a pharmacy problem, hear this: that's not a personal failing. It's a barrier a lot of people hit.
Which brings us to the hopeful number I promised you at the start. It's hiding in the placebo group.
scenes.retention_device: Set up payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: Remember, the placebo group regained fourteen percent on average. But they had lost about twenty-one percent first.
Measured from the very start of the trial, at week eighty-eight the placebo group was still nine point nine percent below their starting weight, on average.

visual.stat_label: Placebo group, weeks 0–88, average weight change

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: The group that stayed on tirzepatide was twenty-five point three percent below their starting weight.

visual.stat_label: Tirzepatide group, weeks 0–88, average weight change

scenes.narration: For Dana, that placebo average would still mean about twenty-two pounds lighter than where she began, even after the regain.
So stopping tended to undo much of the loss, but not all of it, on average. The trial ended at week eighty-eight, so it can't tell us what came after.
The researchers' conclusion: stopping tirzepatide led to substantial regain, while continuing it maintained and added to the weight loss.
Whether long-term treatment is right for you is a conversation for you and your clinician.
So whether you're staying on it or planning a change with your prescriber, what can actually help protect your progress?
Let's be honest about the evidence. No study has proven that a specific habit prevents regain after stopping tirzepatide.
But major expert groups do recommend some foundations, and they're worth building while you're on treatment, not just afterward.
First, strength training. World Health Organization guidelines recommend muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days a week for adults.
A two thousand twenty-five joint advisory from four obesity and nutrition organizations recommends pairing G L P one treatment with resistance training and enough protein, to help protect muscle.
One caveat. If you have kidney disease, your protein target should be set with your clinician or a dietitian, because more isn't automatically better.
The advisory also recommends nutrient-dense, minimally processed foods, including fiber-rich vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains.
Notice the word: recommended. These habits support your health on or off the medicine, but they haven't been proven to prevent regain on their own.

visual.myth: MYTH: Gym and protein guarantee no regain
visual.fact: Recommended for health; not proven to prevent regain

scenes.narration: And if stopping is ever on the table, because of cost, side effects or a life change, plan it with your prescriber rather than alone.

visual.stock_query: two people mapping a plan together

scenes.narration: Questions worth bringing: What should I expect if I stop? What follow-up will I have? Are there other options if cost is the problem? And which numbers should we keep tracking?

items: What should I expect if I stop?
Other options if cost is the problem?
Which numbers do we keep tracking?

scenes.narration: And remember, weight is one health measure among many. Blood pressure, blood sugar, strength, energy, sleep. Progress shows up in more than one number.
Here's your checklist. In SURMOUNT four, people switched to placebo regained fourteen percent on average over a year, yet still ended nine point nine percent below where they started.
Returning hunger is biology, not a character flaw. Stopping is common in real life, and cost and access seem to matter. And strength training plus enough protein are recommended foundations.

items: Stopping is common; cost likely matters
visual.stock_query: three friendly icons in a row

scenes.narration: Picture Dana a year from now. Whatever she decides with her prescriber, she isn't guessing anymore. She knows what the evidence says, and she has a plan.
If this helped you feel a little more in control, subscribe. Every week we turn the newest G L P one research into plain answers like these.

factcheck.summary: Long-form 'What Happens When You Stop Tirzepatide?' is accurate and safe. SURMOUNT-4 figures all check out (783 started; 670 randomized 335/335; mean age 48, ~71% women; no diabetes; −20.9% weeks 0–36; +14.0% vs −5.5% weeks 36–88; 19.4-point gap; 89.5% vs 16.6% kept ≥80% of loss; −25.3% vs −9.9% weeks 0–88; GI side effects mostly mild to moderate during dose escalation). Dana is clearly hypothetical and her maths is consistent. Verified online: Cleveland Clinic study (27% switched, 20% restarted, 14% lifestyle programs, obesity group +0.5% at 1 year, restart/switch explanation is the researchers'), UK study 41.1%, and the US records study (64.8%/46.5%, higher income = less stopping, GI side effects = more stopping). STEP 1 extension, the 2011 diet study, label mechanism and half-life, GLP-1 breakdown by DPP-4, the WHO 2+ days strength advice and the 2025 joint advisory match known sources but weren't opened this session. Observational and secondary results are labelled, the separate-trials caveat is present, there's a kidney caveat on protein, disclaimer and prescriber lines open and close the video, the trial dose mention is design not dosing advice, and the CTA fallback is correct. One optional framing fix in s50 for context on the small real-world regain. Not flagged: S6's drug scope (s47 names only semaglutide and liraglutide; a news summary lists tirzepatide too). Worth checking against the abstract.

issues.claim: Among people treated for obesity, average regain was small, about half a percent, and the researchers think restarting and switching help explain why.
issues.problem: Missing context could make real-world stopping sound almost regain-free. This group had lost only about 8.4% before stopping, stopped within 3–12 months, and 55% did gain weight. That's not comparable to SURMOUNT-4's roughly 21% loss.
issues.fix: Replace the last sentence with: "Among people treated for obesity, who had lost about eight percent before stopping, average regain a year later was small, about half a percent, though more than half did gain some weight. The researchers think restarting and switching help explain why." On screen, change the last list item to: "Obesity group: lost ~8.4%, then about +0.5% at 1 year".

Mascot is tiny relative to the frame.

This looks like an earlier/later scene was reused at the wrong beat, the exact recurring 'one shot = one scripted beat' failure flagged in past QA.

Script calls for a 'SURMOUNT-4 / JAMA, online Dec 2023' citation card here, but the frames show a person with '10-week diet' and 'No medicine' labels under dangling lab-shelf bulbs — content from a different section entirely.

audio.soundNotes: Music under voice already sits at -13.5 dB, right in the target window, so only a gentle +1 dB nudge via gain 1.1 to keep it felt without risking the ceiling. The cue mix is mostly healthy (lots of -14.7 dB speech cues, exactly on target), but about a dozen cues spike well above -14 dB during active narration (notably a bubble at -3.7 dB at 489.3s, a blip/pop pair at -6.1/-5.8 dB at 674s, and a cluster of pops/bubbles around 307s) — these were pulled down 4–10 dB each so they sit felt-not-heard under the voice. Left the big -7 to -9 dB transition swells/whooshes alone since those land in pauses/cuts where that level matches the brief. Added five bespoke story-moment SFX (food-noise stomach murmur at the open, a soft deflating tone on the +14% regain reveal, a quick vanish/poof on 'Gone in minutes', a warm reassuring chime on 'Not a personal failing', and a gentle uplifting bell on 'Continuing maintained the loss') to give the key emotional beats texture the stock kit can't supply, all kept well under voice level.
